passages.t: The nations stream to the mountain of the LORD
passages.happening:
‘In the last days the mountain of the house of the LORD will be established as the chief of the mountains’ (verse 1), raised above the hills, and the peoples will stream to it. Many nations will come and say they will go up to the house of the God of Jacob, so that he will teach them his ways. The law will go out from Zion and the word of the LORD from Jerusalem (verse 2).

He will judge between many peoples. ‘Then they will beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into pruning hooks. Nation will no longer take up the sword against nation, nor will they train anymore for war’ (verse 3). Everyone will sit under his own vine and fig tree, with no one to make him afraid (verse 4). Though the peoples walk in the name of their gods, ‘we will walk in the name of the LORD our God forever and ever’ (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
Right after the verdict that Zion will be plowed comes this vision of Zion raised up. Temples in the ancient world were often built on high places, and mountains were thought of as places where heaven and earth met. The LORD's mountain raised above all others means the God of Israel recognized over every nation. Instead of armies marching up to attack Jerusalem, the nations come as pilgrims to learn. The law that goes out from Zion is torah, instruction in God's ways.

Plowshares were the metal blades of plows, and pruning hooks trimmed vines. Beating weapons into farm tools turns iron and bronze from killing to growing food. To sit under one's own vine and fig tree was a proverbial picture of peace: a family living on its own land, eating its own produce, with no one to take it away. It is the opposite of the land seizures Micah condemned in chapter 2.

These verses appear almost word for word in Isaiah 2:2-4. Scholars debate whether Micah borrowed from Isaiah, Isaiah from Micah, both from an older oracle known in Jerusalem, or whether later editors added it to both. Micah's version adds the vine and fig tree, which fit his country setting.
passages.later: Isaiah has the same vision (Isaiah 2:2-4). The vine and fig tree described the peace of Solomon's reign: ‘each man under his own vine and his own fig tree’ (1 Kings 4:25).
passages.hard:
How can Micah say the nations will beat their swords into plowshares, when war goes on?

Micah places this vision in the last days, a phrase that points to the time when God's purposes are complete, not to a program nations can achieve by treaties alone. Interpreters differ on how it unfolds. Premillennialists expect a future time when Christ reigns on earth and war ceases. Amillennialists and postmillennialists see it beginning now, as the gospel spreads and peace takes root among Christ's people, and completed in the new creation. Others stress that the passage calls God's people to live now as citizens of that coming peace.

The chapter itself holds the vision beside a realistic picture of present conflict (verses 9-13), so it does not deny the reality of war. It declares that war will not have the last word. It belongs to no nation's politics and to no party.
passages.asks: The nations come to Zion to learn, not to fight. Ask what it would look like in your own life to beat a sword into a plowshare. And ask whose name you walk in when others around you walk in the names of their gods.

passages.t: The lame and the outcast gathered
passages.happening:
‘On that day,’ declares the LORD, he will gather the lame and assemble the outcast, even those he has afflicted (verse 6). He will make the lame into a remnant and the outcast into a strong nation, ‘Then the LORD will rule over them in Mount Zion from that day and forever’ (verse 7).

And Zion, the watchtower of the flock, the stronghold of the Daughter of Zion, will have its former rule restored (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
The section opens with On that day, a phrase that points again to the future. God gathers the people no one else wanted: the lame, the scattered, those who have suffered under his own judgment. Out of them he makes a remnant and a strong nation.

The watchtower of the flock translates Migdal-eder, a place near Bethlehem mentioned in Genesis. It is a shepherd's word, and it fits Micah's picture of the LORD as the shepherd who gathers his flock and reigns over it. The former dominion is the kingdom of David, which had been divided and diminished.
passages.later: Jacob pitched his tent beyond the tower of Eder (Genesis 35:21). Zephaniah repeats the promise: ‘I will save the lame and gather the scattered’ (Zephaniah 3:19).
passages.asks: God builds his strong nation out of the lame and the outcast. Ask who your community has left at the edges. And ask whether you are willing to be counted among the weak God gathers.

passages.t: Zion in labor, to Babylon and back
passages.happening:
Why does Zion cry aloud, as if she had no king, gripped by pain like a woman in labor (verse 9)? She is to writhe like a woman giving birth, for she will leave the city and camp in the fields. The promise of verse 10 follows: “You will go to Babylon; there you will be rescued; there the LORD will redeem you from the hand of your enemies!”

Many nations have gathered against Zion, wanting to see her defiled (verse 11). ‘But they do not know the thoughts of the LORD or understand His plan, for He has gathered them like sheaves to the threshing floor’ (verse 12). Zion is told to rise and thresh, and to give what is taken to the Lord of all the earth (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
Verses 9 to 13 hold three short oracles, each beginning with now and each moving from present distress to future rescue. A woman in labor is a picture of pain that carries hope, since labor ends in birth.

Verse 10 names Babylon as the place where Zion will go and be rescued. In Micah's day Assyria was the great power and Babylon a subject city, though often a rebellious one; its king Merodach-baladan sent envoys to Hezekiah, and Isaiah warned then that Judah's treasures and children would be carried to Babylon. Many scholars regard verse 10 as a later addition from the exile after 587 or 586 BC. Others argue that a prophet aware of Babylon's ambitions could have spoken of it, especially beside Isaiah's similar warning. The exile and the return under Cyrus in 539 or 538 BC fulfilled the pattern.

Threshing separated grain from husk. The nations who gather to gloat are themselves gathered like sheaves for God's threshing floor. The picture of horns of iron belongs to that harvest scene. The judgment is God's, and what is taken is given to him. It is no warrant for violence by anyone, and it makes no claim about any nation or conflict today.
passages.later: Isaiah warned Hezekiah that everything in his house would be carried to Babylon (Isaiah 39:6). Ezra tells of the return after Cyrus's decree (Ezra 1:1-4).
passages.asks: The nations did not know the LORD's plan. Ask where you have read a hard season as defeat when God may be at work in it. And ask what it would mean to trust that labor pains can end in new life.
